q: can I give Motrin to my 8 month old for fever
text:
Yes, ibuprofen (Motrin) can be given to a child over 6 months old for fever, according to MedlinePlus [6]. Give it every 6 to 8 hours, and check the packaging or leaflet to make sure the medicine suits your child [2][6]. Know your child's weight before giving it [6].

You can usually look after a fever at home, and it should come down over 1 to 4 days [2]. Offer plenty of fluids — if your baby is breastfed, keep breastfeeding as normal — and give food if they want it [2]. Keep checking on them, including during the night [2].

Get medical advice if you're worried, or if the medicine is not helping [2]. Also get help if your child:
- has a rash along with the fever [1]
- has a fever lasting 5 days or more [1]
- is not eating or not their usual self [1]
- seems dehydrated — fewer wet nappies, sunken eyes, no tears [1]

q: my son threw up twice this morning, what should I give him to drink
text:
Vomiting twice in one morning is often the start of a stomach bug, and the main risk is dehydration [2][1]. The most important thing is to keep fluids going in.

Give an oral rehydration solution. After he vomits, wait 20 minutes, then give 2–5 ml every 5 minutes for an hour, according to the SEUP [3]. If he keeps it down, you can slowly give it more often [3]. Do not use homemade drinks like lemonade or commercial soft drinks [3]. Skip fatty foods, sweets and juices; sports drinks have too much sugar and the wrong electrolytes [4]. You do not need to stop dairy or breastfeeding [4].

Get help if:
- He vomits a lot, cannot keep down solids or liquids, or vomits even without drinking [7]
- The vomit is green, bloody, or looks like coffee grounds [7]
- He is drowsy, limp, very thirsty, has sunken eyes, cries without tears, or urinates little [7]
- He has severe belly pain or a headache [7]
- He is under 3 months and has vomited two or more feeds [7]

q: how do I know if my child is getting dehydrated from vomiting
text:
Dehydration happens when the body loses more fluid than it takes in, and vomiting is one of the common causes [1]. The main risk of vomiting is dehydration, so the priority is to keep fluids going in [3].

When your child vomits, wait 20 minutes, then give oral rehydration solution — 2 to 5 ml every 5 minutes for an hour, according to the SEUP [5]. Watch how well they take it; if they keep it down, you can slowly give it more often [5]. Do not use homemade solutions or fizzy drinks [5]. Oral rehydration fluids you can buy are the most helpful for mild dehydration, and sports drinks without caffeine can help mild cases, according to the CDC [2].

Get help if:
- They seem floppy or very low in energy [3]
- They vomit many times or will not take fluids [3]
- They vomit even when they have not eaten or drunk anything [6]
- The vomit is green, bloody, or looks like brown coffee grounds [6]
- You think they are severely dehydrated [2]

q: my 5 year old has been coughing all night, what can I do
text:
A cough that keeps a child awake at night is common with colds and other respiratory infections, and most children get better on their own [2]. There is no cure for a cold, but you can help your child feel better while it passes: let them rest, offer plenty of fluids, and use a clean humidifier or cool-mist vaporizer in the room [2]. Saline nose drops or spray can also help [2].

Do not give aspirin to a child [2]. Cough and cold medicines often contain ingredients not recommended for children, so talk to your child's doctor before giving any [2]. If you use a separate pain medicine as well, check the labels carefully to avoid a dangerous double dose [2].

Talk to your doctor if your child has trouble breathing or is breathing fast, is dehydrated, has a fever lasting more than 4 days, or symptoms lasting more than 10 days without getting better [2].

q: my son has been coughing for a week after a cold
text:
A cough that lingers for a week or two after a cold is common — cold symptoms can last 10 to 14 days, according to MedlinePlus [6]. If the cough is getting worse instead of better, or comes in bouts, it may be worth having your son checked.

What to do now: keep him comfortable and offer fluids regularly. There is no medicine in these sources for a lingering cough after a cold.

See your doctor if:
- The cough comes in fits lasting minutes, worse at night [4]
- A "whoop" sound when breathing in after coughing [4]
- Vomiting after coughing fits [4]
- Difficulty breathing after a coughing bout [4]
- The cough is getting worse or not improving [2]

For babies under 3 months, coughing bouts, pauses in breathing or turning blue need medical care right away [3].

q: he has a cough but no fever and is eating normally
text:
A cough without fever, with normal eating, is usually a common infection like a cough or cold, according to the NHS [1]. Keep offering fluids and normal meals; a poor appetite for a few days is not harmful [3].

There is no fever here, so fever medicines are not needed. If a fever does appear, the NHS says not to give aspirin to children under 16, not to alternate ibuprofen and paracetamol unless a doctor tells you to, and not to give ibuprofen to a child under 3 months, under 5kg, with chickenpox, dehydrated, or with asthma unless a doctor recommends it [1].

Get help if your child:
- is under 3 months and has a temperature of 38C (100.4 °F) or higher [1]
- has a rash that does not fade when you press a glass against it [1]
- has difficulty breathing, breathlessness or breathing very fast [1]
- is drowsy and hard to wake, or is not responding like they normally do [1]
- is not interested in feeding or normal activities [1]

q: my daughter has red spots all over her stomach and they appeared today
text:
A rash of red spots that appeared today is common in children, and most rashes can be cared for at home. Raised, itchy spots or patches may be hives, which can usually be treated at home, according to the NHS [5].

If it is chickenpox, the spots can be anywhere on the body and may be red, pink or the same colour as the surrounding skin [4]. You can treat it at home: give plenty of fluids (try ice lollies if your child is not drinking), give paracetamol for pain or discomfort, cut your child's fingernails and put socks on their hands at night to stop scratching, use cooling creams or gels, ask a pharmacist about antihistamine medicine for itching, bathe in cool water and pat the skin dry, and dress them in loose clothes [1]. Do not give ibuprofen unless a doctor tells you to, as it may cause serious skin infections, and do not give aspirin to children under 16 [1].

Get help if:
- swelling around the mouth or struggling to breathe [5]
- the spots are painful, or your child seems uncomfortable or distressed [4][6]

q: my 2 year old has little red bumps on his legs and keeps scratching them
text:
Itchy bumps on the legs can have more than one cause, and the pattern matters. Scabies causes severe itching, often worse at night, with itchy bumps and lines on the fingers, wrists, arms, legs and belt area, and a larger rash in small children, according to the WHO [3]. Eczema also causes dry, itchy skin and a rash, and scratching can make it redder and itchier, according to MedlinePlus [2].

Keep the skin from getting scratched: keep nails short and use the treatments your doctor recommends for the skin [2]. For scabies, the diagnosis is made by recognising the typical features, sometimes with a skin examination, and treatment is prescribed by a doctor [5].

See your doctor if:
- The itching is severe or keeps your child awake at night [3]
- You see itchy lines or bumps on the fingers, wrists or belt area [3]
- The skin becomes red, swollen or oozes, which can mean a skin infection [3]
- The rash spreads or does not improve [2]

q: these spots dont seem to bother her but there are more every morning
text:
Spots that don't bother her and keep increasing each morning are most often nappy rash, which is common in babies and can usually be treated at home, according to the NHS [2]. Nappy rash can look like red or raw patches on the bottom or the whole nappy area, or spots, pimples or blisters that may be red or brown [2].

Keep the area clean and dry, change nappies often, and use a barrier cream at each change. If the spots are itchy rather than painless, a pharmacist can advise on antihistamine treatment for hives, though this may not be suitable for young children [7].

Get help if:
- The rash spreads quickly or comes with a fever
- She becomes drowsy, floppy or hard to wake [7]
- Breathing becomes fast or difficult, or lips or tongue swell [7]
- The skin turns blue, grey or pale [7]

If none of these appear and the rash stays limited to the nappy area, it can usually be managed at home [2].

q: my 6 year old fell from the bed and hit the back of his head
text:
Most head injuries in children are not serious, but any symptom needs medical help [2]. After a bang on the head the usual symptoms are headache, confusion, brief memory loss, dizziness, nausea, vomiting and drowsiness, according to the SEUP [1].

At home, keep an eye out for the symptoms listed below. If there is a headache, you can give ibuprofen or paracetamol in the dose your doctor indicates [6]. He can sleep, but after a more significant knock it is worth waking him every 4 hours [6]. No special diet is needed — normal food according to appetite [6]. Rest from sport and screens for 24 to 48 hours, then a gradual return to normal activity [4].

Get help if:
- Intense or worsening headache, or one that does not improve with the usual medicine [4]
- Repeated vomiting [4]
- Confusion or disorientation [4]
- Behaviour change, trouble speaking or walking [4]
- Blood or clear fluid from the nose or ears [4]

The fall was from a bed, so under a metre — but if you are worried about his behaviour or attitude, have him seen [5].

text:
Vomiting once about an hour after a fall is one of the usual symptoms of a head injury, according to the SEUP [7]. Other common signs are headache, confusion, brief memory loss, dizziness, nausea and drowsiness [7].

q: what foods should I start with for a baby who just turned 6 months
text:
Around 6 months, milk alone no longer meets a baby's energy and nutrient needs, so solid foods are needed alongside it, according to the WHO [1]. Start with small amounts and increase them gradually as your baby grows, and keep breastfeeding on demand [1]. Offer a variety of foods, and give 2–3 meals a day at this age [1][2]. How much they eat matters less at first than getting used to eating [2].

Give one new food at a time so you can spot any reaction, such as a rash, diarrhoea or vomiting, according to MedlinePlus [6]. Most babies can have peanut products at around 6 months; ask your doctor if your baby has severe eczema or an egg allergy [6].

Do not give honey, cow's milk, or unpasteurised drinks and foods before 12 months, and no juice before 1 year [6]. Avoid choking hazards like whole nuts, popcorn, hard sweets and whole grapes [6].

q: how much water can a 9 month old drink
text:
For a 9-month-old, breast milk or formula stays the main drink, and water comes on top of that rather than replacing it [2]. Offer it in small amounts with meals and let them drink to thirst; the AEP does not set a fixed daily volume of water at this age [2].

During an illness, offer extra fluids and breastfeed more often, along with soft, favourite foods [1].

A few things to keep in mind:
- No added salt: under 12 months, less than 1 g of salt a day (under 0.4 g of sodium) [3].
- Avoid sugary drinks and commercial fruit juices [3].
- Cow's milk only from 12 months; breast milk remains the first choice [2].

If your baby is unwell, is not feeding, or you are worried about how much they are drinking, contact your doctor.

q: my baby refuses vegetables but eats fruit all day
text: It is common for babies to prefer fruit, and the way to build liking for vegetables is to keep offering them, according to the AEP [2]. Offer the whole variety of fruit and vegetables at any daily meal, and vary how you present them — puréed, mashed or in small pieces [2]. The taste for different flavours, including bitter ones like some vegetables, is formed early, and early exposure to different tastes may reduce the risk of refusing new foods [2]. Include vegetables with iron, such as dark green ones, and offer fruit and vegetables as part of the diet [1]. Give whole fruit rather than fruit juice: juice offers no nutritional benefit over whole fruit, can displace other foods and increases the risk of tooth decay [2]. Keep offering vegetables without forcing, alongside the fruit your baby already enjoys [2].

q: my daughter is 13 months and still mostly drinks formula
text:
At 13 months, formula alone is not enough: from 6 months on, children need complementary foods alongside milk, and breastfeeding is recommended to continue to 2 years or beyond [1]. Complementary feeding means giving solid or liquid foods in addition to breast milk or infant formula, not instead of it [5].

Offer her a variety of soft, mashed family foods several times a day, alongside her formula, so she gets the energy and nutrients milk alone no longer covers [1][5]. The WHO notes that between 12 and 24 months, milk provides about a third of a child's energy needs — the rest has to come from food [6].

If she refuses solids, or you are unsure she is getting enough variety, ask your doctor or a feeding adviser to check her growth and diet [1].

q: how often should a newborn poop
text:
How often a newborn poops varies a lot from baby to baby — the rhythm and consistency of stools differ from one person to another, and it is not essential that a baby has a bowel movement every day, according to the SEUP [3].

What matters more is what the stool is like. Constipation is when stools become too hard, with discomfort or incomplete emptying, and it may come with fewer bowel movements [6]. In a baby this young, keep feeding as usual — breast milk or formula — and do not change the diet [3].

Do not give any laxative or enema without asking your doctor [3].

Get help if:
- Bad tummy pain, or the baby is very floppy and crying a lot [3]
- Blood in the stool [3]
- Vomiting many times, not keeping down milk [3]

Because your baby is under 3 months, any concern about feeding, stools or crying is worth checking with your doctor.

q: my 9 month old suddenly wakes up every two hours at night
text:
It is normal for a 9-month-old to wake at night: night wakings are physiological, and almost 30% of children still wake at night at one year, according to the PUC Chile manual [2]. At this age a night sleep stretch of up to 5 hours is expected [2].

What helps is not intervening so a sleep habit does not form: if they wake, they should settle back to sleep on their own [2]. If a child always falls asleep in your arms, on waking they will want the same conditions to fall asleep again [2]. Sleep cycles last about 90 minutes, and the proportion of REM sleep grows towards the end of the night [2].

Most infant insomnia is due to bad habits [6]. Insomnia itself does not affect growth, though it affects quality of life, causing irritability and lack of attention [6].

The sources do not list warning signs for night wakings in a healthy 9-month-old.

q: my 4 year old wakes up coughing only when he lies down
text:
A cough that comes on at night or when lying down can be a sign of asthma in children, according to MedlinePlus [3]. Asthma symptoms include coughing, especially at night or early morning, chest tightness, and wheezing — a whistling sound when breathing out [3]. In preschool children, the main cause of wheezing is viral respiratory infections, and not every child who wheezes will go on to have asthma, according to the SEUP [4].

See your doctor so they can assess your child. Diagnosing asthma in young children can be difficult, because it looks like other childhood conditions and young children often cannot do the breathing tests; the doctor may suggest trying asthma medicines for several weeks to see if symptoms improve [6].

Get medical help right away if your child has severe coughing, serious breathing problems, or turns very pale or blue in the face, lips or fingernails [3].

q: my son has asthma and is using albuterol more than usual
text:
Using a reliever inhaler more often than usual can be a sign the asthma is not fully controlled, and it is worth having your son seen. Asthma is treated with inhalers: bronchodilators such as salbutamol open the airways and relieve symptoms, while steroid inhalers reduce inflammation and lower the risk of severe attacks [2]. How often an inhaler is needed depends on the frequency of symptoms and the type of inhaler [2].

Give salbutamol with a spacer device (with a mask for small children), never directly into the mouth, as it works less well that way [3][7]. If there is no clear improvement, he should be seen at a health centre [7].

Get help urgently if:
- He is very agitated or drowsy, or turns blue or pale [7]
- Breathing gets worse: faster breathing, ribs showing, chest indrawing [7]
- Inhalations are needed every two hours or less [7]

Take his spacer with you if you go [7].

q: my daughter is breathing faster after running but gets better when she rests

text:
Fast breathing that settles with rest is one of the signs the SEUP lists as worth watching at home, along with ribs pulling in, the chest sinking in, or tiring when walking or running [3]. If your child is otherwise well and has no fever, they can keep up their usual activity, according to the SEUP [3].

Watch at home for:
- General condition getting worse, being listless, sleepy or very irritable [3][4]
- Breathing difficulty: breathing fast, ribs pulling in, chest sinking in [3][4]
- Chest or side pain when breathing [3][4]
- Poor colour [4]
- Refusing food and fluids repeatedly [4]

If any of these appear, the SEUP advises going to the emergency department [3][4].

q: she is making a strange noise when she breathes but is still smiling
text:
A strange noise when breathing can be a sign of croup, which is an inflammation of the voice box and windpipe that often starts like a cold and causes noisy, high-pitched breathing and a barking cough, according to MedlinePlus [3]. It is usually caused by a virus, is more common in children between six months and three years, and most viral cases are mild and can be treated at home [3]. Symptoms often get worse at night and last three to five days [3].

Get help if:
- Breathing becomes difficult or you are worried about it [3]
- The chest caves in, ribs show, or the belly moves with each breath [2][4]
- They seem very drowsy, floppy or very irritable [1][4]
- They refuse to eat or drink [4]
- Their colour looks wrong [4]

Chest pain when breathing deeply can be a sign of asthma, which often also causes a persistent cough (especially at night), wheezing, and shortness of breath or difficulty breathing, sometimes even at rest, according to the WHO [1]. Symptoms can be caused by other conditions too, so a child with symptoms like this should talk to a healthcare provider [1].

- Difficulty breathing, with the ribs pulling in or the chest sinking, fast breathing, or tiring when walking or running [2]

- The child becomes listless, sleepy or very irritable [2][5]
- Poor colour [5]
- Refusing food and fluids repeatedly [5]

q: my daughter is crying nonstop after a fall and wont calm down
text:
A fall on the head can cause headache, confusion, dizziness, nausea, vomiting or drowsiness, and most head injuries in children are mild [1][2]. Crying that will not stop after a blow to the head is a change in behaviour that needs to be checked, according to the SEUP [5].

While you get her seen, keep her calm and do not let her run around or use screens; rest for 24 to 48 hours is recommended after a head injury [6].

Get help now if she has any of these:
- Headache that gets worse or does not go away [4][6]
- Repeated vomiting [4][6]
- Growing confusion, restlessness or agitation [4]
- Hard to wake, or very irritable [6]
- Trouble speaking or walking, weakness in arms or legs [4][6]
- Blood or clear fluid from the nose or ears [6]

Also seek care if the fall was from more than one metre, or if she is under three months old [5].

q: my baby had a seizure last year and has a fever today
text:
A febrile seizure can happen when a child has a high temperature, and it is not usually serious or likely to harm your child or cause long-term effects, according to the NHS [3]. A fever is very common in young children and usually returns to normal within 1 to 4 days [1].

If your child has another seizure: do not move them or try to hold them in place, do not put anything in their mouth, and do not try to lower their temperature by undressing them or sponging them with cold water [5]. Call your local emergency number if the seizure lasts more than 5 minutes, they have difficulty breathing, the stiffness and twitching is on only 1 side, they are more sleepy than usual for more than 1 hour after it stops, or they have more than 1 seizure within 24 hours [2].

Because this would be a seizure, they need to be checked in hospital [6].

q: my 4 year old had a seizure when he was a baby, does that change anything now
text:
A febrile seizure is not usually serious and is unlikely to harm your child or cause long-term effects, according to the NHS [2]. Having had one as a baby does not mean it will happen again, and you cannot prevent them [3].

If your child ever has another seizure, keep them safe while you wait for help: check the time it starts and ends, protect their head with your hands or something soft, and move dangerous objects away [4]. Do not hold them still, put anything in their mouth, or try to cool them with cold water or by undressing them [1]. After it ends, put them in the recovery position [4].

Get medical help if a seizure lasts more than 5 minutes, they have trouble breathing, twitching is on only one side, they stay sleepier than usual for over an hour afterwards, or they have more than one seizure in 24 hours [5].

q: my 7 year old says her neck hurts with a fever
text:
A fever with a stiff neck needs urgent medical attention, according to the NHS [7]. While you get help, keep your child calm and do not give them aspirin [7].

A stiff neck is one of the signs that mean calling your local emergency number right away [7]. Other signs to watch for at the same time:

- Being bothered by light [7]
- A fit (febrile seizure) for the first time [7]
- Drowsy and hard to wake, or confused [7]
- Difficulty breathing, or unusually cold hands and feet [7]

Do not undress your child or sponge them down to cool them, and do not cover them in too many clothes or bedclothes [7].

q: my child has a sore throat and white stuff on the tonsils
text:
A sore throat with white patches on the tonsils is often tonsillitis, an infection of the tonsils that is a common childhood illness [1]. The white patches can also be pus-filled spots, which are one of the more severe symptoms [1].

To help soothe it: offer plenty of water, cool or soft foods, and rest. Children should not gargle with salt water, and do not give young children ice cubes, ice lollies or hard sweets to suck because of the risk of choking [6]. A pharmacist can suggest treatments such as lozenges, throat sprays or antiseptic solutions [2].

Get medical help now if:
- Pus-filled spots on the tonsils [2]
- A sore throat so painful it is hard to eat or drink [2]
- A severe sore throat that quickly gets worse [3]
- Difficulty speaking, swallowing, breathing or opening the mouth [3]
- Swelling inside the mouth and throat [3]

See a doctor if the symptoms do not go away within a week or the throat infections keep coming back [2].

q: when should I take my kid to the doctor for a sore throat
text:
Sore throats are very common and usually nothing to worry about — they normally get better by themselves within a week, according to the NHS [5]. Most are caused by viruses like a cold or flu [3].

To soothe it: drink plenty of water, eat cool or soft foods, suck ice cubes or ice lollies (nothing small and hard for young children, because of choking), and rest [5]. Gargling with warm salty water helps adults, but children should not try it [5]. Paracetamol or ibuprofen can relieve the pain — ask a pharmacist about these [6]. Children should not take aspirin [1].

See a doctor if:
- Your child is under 5 and needs help for a sore throat [2]
- It does not improve after a week [2]
- A very high temperature, or feeling hot, cold or shivery [2]
- Signs of dehydration — peeing less than usual, or dark, strong-smelling pee [2]
- A lump in the mouth or neck, or a mouth ulcer lasting more than 3 weeks [2]

Get help immediately if your child has difficulty breathing or cannot swallow, is drooling, or makes a high-pitched sound when breathing [2].

q: my son has been scratching his scalp and has white flakes
text:
White flakes on the scalp with itching are most often dandruff, a common condition that is not harmful and cannot be caught from anyone else [6]. It is not caused by poor hygiene, though it can be more noticeable if the hair is not washed regularly [1].

Wash your son's hair regularly with a gentle shampoo, and see your doctor if things do not get better in a month [1].

Get help if:
- Scaly, itchy, red patches spread to the face or other areas of the body [1]
- A red or silver rash on the scalp, sometimes with patchy hair loss [1]
- Red, flaky, crusty patches covered with silvery scales [1]
- Greasy, yellowish crusts on the scalp, eyebrows or nappy area [1]

If the flakes are greasy and yellowish rather than dry and white, that points to cradle cap, which is harmless and usually goes away on its own within a few months [4].

q: my 3 year old was stung by a bee on the hand
text:
A bee sting is a common cause of allergic reactions, and most stay mild, according to MedlinePlus [2]. Watch the hand for swelling, itching or a rash, which are the usual signs of an allergic reaction [2].

For a mild sting, keep the hand clean and cool, and give paracetamol or ibuprofen if it hurts — the dose depends on your child's weight, and PediBot's dose calculator covers both [3].

Get help if any of these appear, as they can mean a serious reaction (anaphylaxis) starting within minutes [4]:
- Itching or hives spreading over the body [4]
- Swelling of the eyelids, lips or ears [4]
- Trouble breathing, cough or wheezing [4]
- Dizziness, fainting or vomiting [4]
- Intense redness all over [4]

A severe reaction can affect the whole body and become life-threatening, so it needs emergency care straight away [1][4].

q: my son got a small burn from hot water on his arm
banner: 🚨 With these symptoms your child should be seen in the emergency department today, without waiting. | Reason: Burn (especially face, hands, genitals or large area)
text:
Small burns and scalds can often be treated at home, according to the NHS [2]. Hold the burn under cool running water for 20 minutes, as soon as possible and within 3 hours of it happening [3]. q: my baby has a temperature of 100.4, is that considered a fever
text:
100.4 °F = 38 °C.

If your baby is under 3 months old, a temperature of 100.4 °F needs a doctor the same day.

For an older baby, yes — that counts as a fever. A normal temperature is usually around 98.6 °F (37 °C (98.6 °F)), and a fever is a temperature higher than normal, according to MedlinePlus [6]. A fever is not a disease; it is usually a sign the body is fighting an infection [6].

You can usually look after them at home. Give plenty of fluids — if your baby is breastfed, keep breastfeeding as normal — and check on them regularly, including during the night, according to the NHS [2]. If they are distressed or uncomfortable, you can give paracetamol or ibuprofen, checking the packaging or leaflet to be sure the medicine suits your child [2]. The dose depends on their age and weight, so follow the leaflet or ask your doctor.

Get medical advice if:
- They are under 3 months old with a temperature of 100.4 °F (38 °C (100.4 °F)) or higher [5]
- They are 3 to 6 months old with a temperature of 102.2 °F (39 °C (102.2 °F)) or higher [5]
- They have a rash along with the fever [5]
- The fever has lasted 5 days or more [5]
- They are not feeding or not themselves, and you are worried [5]

If your child is under 3 months old, a fever needs a doctor the same day.

- A stiff neck, or a severe headache that is getting worse

- Cold hands and feet, or skin that is blue, grey, pale or blotchy
- Vomiting, or a fit (seizure)

q: how many wet diapers should a 4 month old have
text:
A 4-month-old should usually have at least 6 wet diapers in 24 hours, though this can vary. According to MedlinePlus, a baby may be dehydrated if they do not wet their diapers for 3 hours or more [1].

If you are worried about dehydration, watch for these signs:
- Dry mouth and tongue [1]
- Crying without tears [1]
- No wet diaper for 3 hours or more [1]
- Unusual sleepiness or irritability [1]
- Sunken eyes [1]

q: can babies get dehydrated from breastfeeding
banner: 🚨 With these symptoms your child should be seen in the emergency department today, without waiting. | Reason: Signs of dehydration: sunken eyes, little urine, dry mouth, persistent vomiting or heavy diarrhoea >24 h
text:
Breastfeeding does not cause dehydration — it protects against it. The WHO lists exclusive breastfeeding for the first six months as one of the key measures to prevent diarrhoeal illness, and says breastfeeding should continue during episodes of diarrhoea [5].

If your baby is losing fluids through vomiting or diarrhoea, keep breastfeeding normally, and even more often if your baby wants it [3]. Offer smaller amounts more frequently to reduce the risk of vomiting [3]. Oral rehydration solution is what replaces the water and salts lost, and it is absorbed in the small intestine [5]; it is used to prevent and treat dehydration caused by vomiting or diarrhoea, including in infants [4]. Avoid sports drinks, sweets and juices — they have too much sugar and the wrong electrolytes for a child with diarrhoea [3].

Get help if your baby vomits a lot or cannot keep down solids or liquids, or if the vomit is green, bloody or looks like coffee grounds [3].

q: should I give my daughter the HPV vaccine
text:
The HPV vaccine protects against human papillomavirus, a common virus spread through skin contact, usually during sex. Some types are linked to an increased risk of several cancers, including cervical, mouth, anal, penile, vulval and vaginal cancer, and genital warts [1]. It works very well: since it has been used, there has been a big drop in young people getting conditions linked to HPV, such as cervical cancer and genital warts [2].

In the United States, the ages and doses for the HPV vaccine follow the national schedule, so ask your doctor when your daughter is due.

The most common side effects are mild and do not last long: swelling or pain where the injection was given, headache, a high temperature, dizziness, feeling sick, tiredness [5]. A severe allergic reaction is very rare, and the person who vaccinates is trained to treat it immediately [5].

q: my 11 year old needs a tetanus shot after a cut, does he need one
text:
Tetanus enters the body through cuts or wounds, and vaccination is how it is prevented [1][4]. An 11-year-old is past the age for DTaP, which is only for children younger than 7; older children and teens get Tdap or Td instead [1]. Whether a booster is needed after a cut depends on how many tetanus-containing doses he has already had and how long ago the last one was — that is a decision for his doctor, who can check his record and give the right vaccine [1].

Tell the vaccination provider if he has ever had an allergic reaction to a tetanus, diphtheria or pertussis vaccine, a coma or prolonged seizures within 7 days of a pertussis vaccine, a seizure or other nervous system problem, Guillain-Barré syndrome, or severe pain or swelling after a previous tetanus or diphtheria dose [1][3].

After any shot, soreness or swelling where it was given, fever, tiredness, fussiness, loss of appetite and vomiting can happen [3].

- Your child has symptoms [1]

If you are told to go to the emergency department, do not drive yourself — ask someone to drive you [5].

q: my daughter is 13 and started her period but has very heavy bleeding
banner: 🚨 Call 911 now or go to the emergency department. | Reason: Deep wound with heavy bleeding that does not stop after 10 minutes of pressure
text:
Heavy periods are common in the first years after a girl's first period, and about half of all teenage girls have irregular periods in the first year after their first period, according to the WHO [3]. The main complication to watch for is anaemia, which can be serious but is rarely fatal [3].

A normal period lasts 2 to 7 days, comes every 21 to 35 days, and the blood is dark red and does not clot [2][3]. Bleeding that is heavier or longer than this is considered abnormal [2].

What to do now: eat iron-rich foods such as lean red meat, fish, poultry, lentils, beans, fortified cereals and dark leafy greens, and foods rich in vitamin C, which help the body absorb iron [7]. Avoid tea, coffee, cocoa and bran with iron-rich meals, as they slow iron absorption [7].

Get help from your doctor:
- Bleeding that is excessive in amount or lasts longer than normal [2]
- Periods coming more often than every 21 days [2]
- Signs of anaemia, such as tiredness or pallor [7]

Girls with heavy menstrual bleeding should see a doctor for treatment; doctors may recommend iron supplements or hormonal contraceptives [7].

q: my child says his heart is beating really fast after an energy drink
text:
A fast heartbeat after an energy drink is a heart palpitation: the heartbeat becomes noticeable and may feel like it is racing or beating very fast, and it can last seconds, minutes or longer [3]. Energy drinks contain caffeine, and caffeine is one of the things that can set off this kind of symptom [6].

Get help if the fast heartbeat keeps coming back or if there are other symptoms along with it [3].

Seek urgent care if any of these appear:
- The child has symptoms after the drink [7]
- You are unsure what was in the drink or how much was taken [7]
- The symptoms do not settle [7]

If you go, take the can or bottle with you [7].

q: my child has asthma but is not wheezing right now, should I still use albuterol
text:
No, if there is no wheeze or trouble breathing right now, the sources describe salbutamol as a treatment for an asthma attack — the episodes of cough, breathlessness and wheezing caused by narrowed airways — not as something to give when the child is well [1]. Asthma symptoms come and go over time, and it can be managed with the right treatment [2].

When an attack does come, the SEUP says to give 2 to 4 puffs of salbutamol one at a time through a spacer (with a face mask for small children), and repeat that dose after 10 to 15 minutes [6]. Keep the child resting, away from tobacco smoke, and continue any maintenance treatment during the attack [6].

Get help if:
- Very agitated or drowsy, or turning blue or pale [7]
- Breathing getting faster, ribs or chest pulling in [7]
- Needing puffs every two hours or less [7]
- No clear improvement after treatment at home [6]

If you are unsure whether to treat, ask your doctor or asthma team.

q: I found a lump behind my baby's ear, should I worry
banner: 🚨 With these symptoms your child should be seen in the emergency department today, without waiting. | Reason: Swelling or redness behind the ear, or the ear pushed forward: it should be seen today
text:
A lump behind the ear is not one of the usual signs of an ear infection. Ear infections are very common in children and often get better on their own within 3 days, according to the NHS [2]. The usual signs are earache, a high temperature, difficulty hearing, discharge from the ear, or a baby rubbing or pulling their ear, being irritable or off their food [2][4].

While you are getting your baby seen, you can keep them comfortable: treat the pain with ibuprofen or paracetamol every 6-8 hours, given regularly for the first 1-2 days, and do not put anything in the ear to calm the pain, according to the SEUP [3]. If your baby is a infant, frequent nasal washes with saline help [3]. It is normal for them to have little appetite, so do not force them to eat [3].

Get help sooner if:
- Poor general condition, intense headache, drowsy or very irritable [5]
- Redness, pain or swelling behind the ear, or the ear pushed forward [5]
- Fever of 39°C (102.2 °F) or higher, or pus from the ear [5]
- No improvement after 48-72 hours of pain treatment [5]

q: my toddler has a swollen eyelid after waking up
text:
A swollen eyelid on waking is one of the early signs of roseola, a very common infection in babies and toddlers that usually causes a high temperature and a rash, according to the NHS [3]. It normally gets better at home within about a week [3].

Keep your child comfortable and offer plenty to drink. The swollen eyelids and swollen neck glands, along with cold-like symptoms, usually last 3 to 5 days before a rash appears [3]. The rash starts on the chest, tummy and back, then spreads to the face, neck and arms, and usually fades within 2 days [3].

See your doctor if:
- Your child seems very unwell or is not drinking
- The swelling spreads to the lips, tongue or throat
- Breathing becomes difficult or noisy [6]
- Your child becomes pale or loses consciousness [6]

Swelling of the eyelids can also be part of a serious allergic reaction, so get medical help straight away if it comes with trouble breathing, widespread rash or vomiting [6].

q: my child has a fever but his hands are freezing cold
banner: 🚨 With these symptoms your child should be seen in the emergency department today, without waiting. | Reason: Cold hands and feet in a child with fever: it may be poor circulation, get it checked
text:
If your child is under 3 months old, a fever needs a doctor the same day. For an older child, cold hands and feet with a fever are common: the body is raising its temperature and the blood vessels in the skin narrow, which is why the hands and feet feel cold [7]. This is part of how fever works, not a sign on its own that something is wrong.

What to do now: check the temperature with a thermometer, under the arm is fine [5]. If there are no warning signs, start with physical measures — take off extra clothing, offer plenty of fluids, reduce activity, and a lukewarm bath only if the child is comfortable [5]. Do not undress or sponge the child to cool them, and do not wrap them in too many clothes or blankets [2]. If the child is uncomfortable with a fever above 38°C (100.4 °F), give the antipyretic your paediatrician usually recommends [6]; the dose depends on their age and weight.

Get help if:
- The child is floppy, barely responsive or very irritable [1]
- Difficulty breathing [1]
- Spots that do not fade when pressed [1]
- Not keeping down solids or liquids [1]
- Under 2 months old or immunocompromised [1]

q: my son fell yesterday and now he is acting confused
banner: 🚨 Call 911 now or go to the emergency department. | Reason: Drowsy after a knock or a fall: call emergency services or go to the emergency department now
text:
A knock on the head is a common injury, and the skull usually protects the brain [4]. After a head injury, keep your son resting — no sport, no screens — for 24 to 48 hours, then return to normal activities gradually, according to the SEUP [5].

Confusion after a head injury is a warning sign, not an expected effect: get him checked now [4][5]. While you get help, keep him with you and do not leave him alone [5].

Signs that need urgent help, from MedlinePlus [4]:
- Confusion that is getting worse, or restlessness
- Vomiting or nausea again and again
- A headache that gets worse or does not go away
- Trouble speaking, or weakness or numbness in arms or legs
- Trouble waking up, or not able to stand up

The SEUP also says to go to the emergency department if your child is under three months, or if the fall was from more than one metre [3].

q: she hit her head last week and has been completely normal until today
text:
Most head injuries are not serious, but it's important to get medical help for any symptoms, according to the NHS [3]. A concussion is a temporary brain injury that can last a few weeks [3].

Because the injury was a week ago and she has been well until today, she should be seen. Get medical help now for any of these:

- Being sick (vomiting) [3]
- Feeling dizzy [3]
- Problems with walking, balance, understanding, speaking or writing [3]
- New numbness or weakness anywhere [3]
- Any other symptom that worries you [3]

While you arrange that, let her rest and keep her away from sport, rough play and screens; the SEUP advises physical and mental rest for 24 to 48 hours after a knock, then a gradual return to normal activity [2]. If she has a headache, the SEUP says paracetamol or ibuprofen can be given in the dose your doctor indicates [5]. She can sleep, and eat as normal [5].

q: my child says he feels like he cant catch his breath but his oxygen monitor says 99
text:
A monitor reading of 99 means the oxygen level in the blood is normal, but it does not rule out a breathing problem — a child can feel short of breath while their oxygen still reads fine. The SEUP says to watch for difficulty breathing at home: the ribs pulling in or the chest sinking, breathing fast, getting tired when walking or running, or chest pain when breathing [2].

If you can see any of those, or your child's general state is worse — limp, sleepy or very irritable — the SEUP says to go to the emergency department [2]. The same applies if there is difficulty breathing, a bad colour, or they keep refusing food and fluids, according to the SEUP [5].

Trust what you see in your child over the number on the monitor. If you are worried about your child's breathing, MedlinePlus says to call your doctor straight away [4].

q: my daughter is breathing fast because she is crying, should I be worried
banner: 🚨 With these symptoms your child should be seen in the emergency department today, without waiting. | Reason: Breathing difficulty: fast breathing, wheezing, ribs pulling in
text:
Fast breathing while crying is expected — crying itself makes a child breathe faster, and cold-like symptoms are very common in babies and children and are not usually a sign of anything serious [2]. What matters is how she breathes once she has settled.

Once she is calm, watch her breathing for a minute. Signs that need attention are breathing much faster than usual, long gaps between breaths, the ribs pulling in or the chest dipping, noisy breathing, or difficulty feeding [2][5]. Also watch her general state: if she becomes floppy, sleepy or very irritable, or has chest pain when breathing [3][4].

If any of those appear, she needs to be seen. If you are worried she is seriously ill, get medical help [2].

While you wait, keep her upright and calm, and offer small sips or feeds often if she will take them [2].

q: my child has a fever and I can feel his heart beating very fast
text:
If your child is under 3 months old, a fever needs a doctor the same day. For an older child: a fever is very common in young children, and the temperature usually returns to normal within 1 to 4 days, according to the NHS [2]. A high temperature is 38C (100.4 °F) or more; check it with a digital thermometer in the armpit, and if they have just had a bath or been wrapped in a blanket, wait a few minutes and try again [2].

A fast heartbeat during a fever can be a sign of sepsis, which is a medical emergency — people who may have it should seek medical care right away, according to the WHO [5]. Other signs to look for include confusion, difficulty breathing, clammy and sweaty skin, extreme body pain, or, in children, fast breathing, convulsions, pale skin, lethargy, difficulty waking up, or feeling cold to the touch [5]. In children under 5, it can also cause difficulty feeding, frequent vomiting or lack of urination [5].

Do not give any specific dose — it depends on your child's age and weight.

How old is your child? With the age I can make this more precise.

q: my 3 year old has had a fever since yesterday but is drinking and peeing
text:
A fever with drinking and peeing normally is a good sign, but a fever in a 3-year-old can be a sign of a urinary tract infection, so it is worth having your child seen [3][6].

Keep offering fluids often so they keep drinking and peeing [5]. If your child seems uncomfortable, a painkiller can help — the dose depends on their weight [4].

See your doctor if your child:
- has a high temperature or feels hot and shivery [6]
- seems generally unwell, irritable, or is not feeding, eating or drinking properly [6]
- is sick (vomiting) [6]
- wets the bed or themselves [6]
- has pain in the lower tummy or back, or blood in their pee [1]

Your doctor can check for a UTI with a urine test and treat it with antibiotics if needed [3].

text:
A cough that brings up vomit can happen with whooping cough, or pertussis: the coughing fits can be violent enough to make a child vomit, according to MedlinePlus [3]. It usually starts like a cold — runny nose, mild fever, an occasional cough — and the worse coughing fits come after a week or two [2].

What to do now: keep offering fluids in small sips often, and keep the child away from smoke or fumes, which can set off the cough [1]. If your child is diagnosed with pertussis, antibiotics may shorten how long they can pass it on [4].

Get help if:
- Your child has pauses in breathing or turns blue [2]
- Breathing becomes difficult after a coughing fit [5]
- The coughing fits keep getting worse or more frequent [2]
- Your child seems exhausted after coughing fits [2]

Coughing fits can last up to 10 weeks or more, and recovery is slow [2].

q: my baby has red cheeks but no fever
text:
Red cheeks on their own, without a fever, are not a sign of illness. A high temperature is usually considered to be 38C (100.4 °F) (100.4F) or above, and flushed cheeks are one of the things that can go with it, according to the NHS [2]. If you think your baby may have a high temperature, check it with a digital thermometer — that is the most accurate way for a baby or young child [7].

If the cheeks are just red and your baby is otherwise well, there is nothing you need to treat. Spots that appear on a baby's cheeks, forehead, chin, scalp or upper body up to 6 weeks after birth could be baby acne, which does not need treatment and usually gets better after a few weeks or months [5].

Get medical advice if your baby:
- feels hotter than usual on their back or chest [2]
- feels sweaty or clammy [2]
- seems unwell in any other way [2]

q: my son is 4 and weighs 25 pounds, is that too little
text:
25 lb = 11.3 kg.

Growth is judged by plotting weight and height on the WHO growth charts for his age and sex, not by the number alone [2]. The charts let health workers spot underweight or overweight early, before a child crosses a threshold [2]. For children under 5, weight-for-height is used to define wasting (low weight for height) and excess weight, and weight-for-age is used for weight deficit in the first year [4]. A single measurement is not enough: what matters is the trend over time on his own curve, and a change in that curve is a warning sign that needs looking at [5]. q: my 18 month old only says a few words
text:
At 18 months, saying only a few words can be within the normal range, but it is also a sign worth checking. The PUC Chile manual lists "no dice alguna palabra" (not saying any word) at 18 months as a warning sign of psychomotor delay [2], and notes that at a year and a half children typically have 20–30 words [4]. First words usually appear around 12 months, and two-word phrases around 24 months [3].

What to do now: ask your doctor to assess your child's language milestones at a routine visit. The manual says health teams should clinically evaluate developmental milestones at routine check-ups, and that scales such as Denver or Bayley can be used for screening [1][5]. Your child's hearing should also be checked, since not turning to sound can point to a hearing problem [2].

Get help if:
- No words at all by 18 months [2]
- No babbling or gestures like pointing or waving by 12 months [2]
- Loss of language or social skills at any age [2]
- No independent walking by 18 months [2]

q: my son has a rash after swimming in a lake
text:
A rash that appears after swimming in a lake is often hives (urticaria): raised, itchy bumps or patches that can appear anywhere on the body and change shape or move around [1][4]. In children, most hives are caused by an infection, and an allergic cause is less common [4].

What to do now:
- Don't rub the skin, and avoid very hot baths or showers [5].
- Don't put powders or creams on the skin, or give any syrup, without checking with your child's doctor first [5].
- They can eat their usual food; you don't need to introduce new foods [5].
- A pharmacist can advise on antihistamine treatment for the rash, though it may not be suitable for young children [7].

Get help straight away if:
- The lips, mouth, throat or tongue suddenly swell [7]
- Breathing is very fast or struggling, or the throat feels tight [7]
- The skin, tongue or lips turn blue, grey or pale [7]
- They suddenly become very confused, drowsy or dizzy [7]
- A child is limp, floppy or not responding normally [7]

q: what should I know about malaria symptoms in a child returning from Africa
text:
Malaria is a potentially deadly disease spread by mosquito bites, and children under 5 are at higher risk of severe infection, according to the WHO [1]. Early symptoms are often mild and easy to mistake for other fevers: fever, headache and chills, usually appearing 10 to 15 days after an infected bite [2]. Because the symptoms are not specific, get a test as soon as possible [2]. Early treatment of a mild case can stop it getting worse [2].

Severe signs to watch for:
- Extreme tiredness and fatigue [2]
- Confusion or reduced awareness [2]
- Seizures [2]
- Difficulty breathing [2]
- Dark or bloody urine, yellow eyes or skin, unusual bleeding [2]

Anyone with severe symptoms needs emergency care quickly [2].

q: my child coughs mostly at night but is fine during the day
text:
A cough that is mostly at night and fine during the day can be a sign of asthma in children: the SEUP says children may have a cough, sometimes at night, along with a feeling of breathlessness [6]. Asthma is a long-term condition of the airways that can cause wheezing, cough and chest tightness [4].

What to do now: keep a note of when the cough happens — at night, after exercise, or after a cold — because that pattern helps your doctor. Diagnosing asthma in young children can be hard, since the symptoms look like other childhood illnesses and some children do not have symptoms often [3]. Your doctor may examine your child, ask about the history, and in younger children may suggest trying asthma medicines for several weeks to see if the symptoms improve [3].

Get help if:
- Your child's lips or face turn blue or grey [6]
- Your child is breathing fast, or the chest and ribs pull in when breathing [6]
- Your child has severe breathlessness, constant cough, or trouble speaking [6]
- You are worried about your child's breathing [5]

q: my son has had a dry cough for three weeks
text:
A cough that lasts three weeks or more is a reason to have your son examined for tuberculosis, according to the Ministério da Saúde [1]. The main symptom of pulmonary TB is cough, which can be dry or productive, and anyone with a cough for three weeks or more should be checked [1]. Take him to your nearest health centre for evaluation and tests; if the result is positive, treatment should start as soon as possible and be followed to the end [1].

Because he is under 3 months old, do not give any cough or cold medicine at home — talk to your child's health professional before giving any medicine for cough or cold [5].

Get help if:
- Trouble breathing or fast breathing [5]
- Symptoms lasting more than 10 days without improvement [5]
- Symptoms that improve but then come back or get worse [5]
- Fever lasting more than 4 days [5]

q: my daughter has a wet cough but no fever
text:
A wet cough without a fever is usually caused by a common infection of the airways, and fever is not always part of it [1]. Give plenty of fluids to prevent dehydration [2]. If the cough is bothering them, keep them comfortable and let them rest; there is no need to wake a sleeping child to give medicine [6].

- is not their usual self and you're worried [1]
- does not want to eat [1]
- is dehydrated — nappies not very wet, sunken eyes, no tears when crying [1]
- has difficulty breathing, breathlessness or is breathing very fast [1]

text:
A cough after choking can be a sign that something is still in the airway, so it needs checking. The NHS says to get help if a child is struggling to breathe — choking, gasping or unable to speak — or has pale, blue or blotchy skin, lips or tongue [3]. If they are breathing normally now, still have them seen today: a cough that follows a choking episode is not something to watch at home. Go to the emergency department or call your local emergency number.

- struggling to breathe, gasping or unable to speak [3]
- pale, blue or blotchy skin, lips or tongue [3]
- sudden confusion or floppiness, or not waking [3]
- coughing up blood [3]

q: my daughter fainted for a few seconds at school and feels fine now
text:
A brief fainting spell (syncope) is a sudden, short loss of consciousness, usually because not enough blood or oxygen reached the brain [2]. It often happens with heat, pain, fear, anxiety, standing still a long time, or getting up suddenly [2]. After a period of rest, children usually recover quickly, within a couple of minutes [5].

What to do now: have her sit or lie down at once if she feels unwell again, and breathe slowly and deeply [5]. If she faints, lay her with her legs raised and her head to one side so she breathes better [5]. When the weakness has passed, she can sit up slowly, then stand after a few minutes [5]. Encourage her to drink more fluids, especially with exercise [4].

Get help if:
- She takes more than 3–5 minutes to come round [6]
- It happened during exercise, effort, or while sitting [6]
- It came with palpitations, chest pain, jerking limbs, or wetting herself [6]

q: mi hijo tiene fiebre despues de las vacunas
text:
Si el bebé tiene menos de 3 meses, la fiebre necesita que lo vea un médico ese mismo día.

En un niño mayor, la fiebre después de las vacunas es un efecto esperado y pasajero. Los prematuros y los recién nacidos de riesgo deben vacunarse según su edad cronológica, sin retrasar el calendario, y la seguridad de las vacunas es en general similar a la de los niños nacidos a término [3]. Las edades y dosis de las vacunas siguen el calendario nacional de Estados Unidos.

Qué hacer ahora:
- Ofrécele líquidos con frecuencia y ropa ligera.
- Si tiene fiebre y malestar, puedes darle paracetamol o ibuprofeno; la dosis depende de su peso y su edad, así que consúltala con tu médico o en el prospecto.
- No retrases las próximas vacunas por esta fiebre [3].

Consulta a tu médico si:
- Tiene menos de 3 meses y fiebre [3].
- La fiebre dura varios días o sube mucho.
- Está decaído, irritable o no come.
- Aparecen manchas en la piel, vómitos o dificultad para respirar.

Los grandes prematuros (menos de 32 semanas) pueden tener pausas de respiración o el pulso lento en las 48-72 horas siguientes, sobre todo si siguen hospitalizados [3].

¿Qué edad tiene? Con la edad afino la respuesta.

q: my 18 month old has a fever of 103 and won't take Tylenol
text:
103 °F = 39.4 °C.

A fever is usually a sign the body is fighting an infection, and most fevers in young children settle within 1 to 4 days, according to the NHS [5]. The goal is your child's comfort, not the number on the thermometer [3].

Keep offering plenty of fluids in small sips, dress them lightly, and do not bundle them up or sponge them with cold water — that is unpleasant and does not help [3][5]. It is normal for them to refuse food; do not force it [3].

If they will not take Tylenol, you can try acetaminophen every 4 to 6 hours, or ibuprofen every 6 to 8 hours, dosed by your child's weight [4]. Never give aspirin to a child [4].

Get help if your child:
- has a seizure or fit [5]
- is floppy, confused or hard to wake [5]
- has trouble breathing [5]
- has a rash that does not fade when pressed [5]
- is not drinking or has fewer wet nappies [3]

q: can I give him both Tylenol and Motrin at the same time
text:
Yes, you can give them together if a doctor or nurse tells you to — but do not do it on your own. The usual advice is to give one, and if it is not helping, switch to the other instead of giving both at once [2]. If a health professional does advise alternating them, write down the time of each dose so the doses stay evenly spaced and your child does not get too much [2].

Acetaminophen (Tylenol) is given every 4 to 6 hours, and ibuprofen (Motrin) every 6 to 8 hours [1]. Ibuprofen is not for children under 6 months [1]. Know your child's weight before giving either one [1].

Call your doctor before giving both together, or if you are unsure which to use.

q: why does my 3 year old have a temperature of 105 degree celsius

q: my 5 year old won't stop itching her arms and legs at night
text:
Itchy skin at night that is worse in the evening can be scabies, an itchy rash caused by mites that spreads through close skin contact and should be treated quickly to stop it spreading, according to the NHS [5]. Scabies causes severe itch, often worse at night, with itchy lines and bumps on the fingers, wrists, arms and legs, and a larger rash in small children including the palms, soles and scalp, according to the WHO [2].

See your doctor, because scabies needs treatment and everyone in the household usually needs treating at the same time [5].

Get help if:
- The itch is severe or keeps your child awake at night [2]
- You see itchy lines or bumps on the fingers, wrists, arms or legs [2]
- The skin becomes infected, with sores or crusting [2]
- Your child has a weakened immune system [2]

q: how long does flu last in toddlers
text:
Most children get better from flu on their own, and the illness usually passes in a few days [6]. While your toddler has it, keep them at home so they don't pass it on, let them rest, and offer plenty to drink [6]. Treat other symptoms like fever as usual [6].

Get medical attention if their symptoms get worse [6]. Children under five are among those at higher risk of complications, so if you are worried, contact your doctor [6].

For a toddler, the cough and runny nose of a cold-like illness can last longer than the fever: fever usually settles in two or three days, while cough can go on more than a week [5]. Offer fluids often, and if they have a fever over 38°C (100.4 °F) and are uncomfortable, give the usual anti-fever medicine your paediatrician recommends [5].

q: can my 10 year old take adult Tylenol if I cut it in half
text:
No — do not cut an adult Tylenol in half for a 10-year-old. Acetaminophen (Tylenol) helps reduce fever in children and adults, but the amount you give depends on your child's weight, not on halving an adult tablet [1]. Know how much your child weighs before giving it, and give acetaminophen every 4 to 6 hours [1].

Check the packet or leaflet to see if it is suitable for your child, and speak to a pharmacist or doctor if you are not sure [3]. Paracetamol may not be suitable if your child has had an allergic reaction to it before or has a kidney or liver condition [3].

Do not give your child any other medicine that also contains paracetamol, such as cold and flu medicine [4].

If you have given more than the packet, leaflet or prescription says, get medical advice, because it can sometimes be dangerous [6].

q: my 14 year old says her throat hurts really bad when swallowing
text:
A sore throat that hurts when swallowing is very common and usually nothing to worry about — it normally gets better by itself within a week, according to the NHS [5]. It is often caused by a virus like a cold or flu [4].

To help soothe it: drink plenty of water, eat cool or soft foods, suck ice cubes, ice lollies or hard sweets, rest, and avoid smoking or smoky places [5]. She is old enough to gargle with warm, salty water — half a teaspoon of salt in a glass of warm water, gargle and spit it out, do not swallow [5].

Antibiotics are not usually needed, because they will not normally relieve the symptoms or speed up recovery [7].

See a doctor if:
- The sore throat does not improve after a week [7]
- You are worried about her symptoms [7]
- She has a very high temperature, or feels hot, cold or shivery [7]
- She has signs of dehydration, such as peeing less than usual or dark, strong-smelling pee [7]

Get help now if she has difficulty breathing or cannot swallow, is drooling, or is making a high-pitched sound as she breathes [7].

q: why do I have a fever and chills today
text:
A fever is usually a sign your body is fighting an infection, not an illness in itself — most fevers are caused by infections, and the fever is part of how your body kills the virus or bacteria behind it [2]. Chills often come with it [4].

Drink enough fluids to prevent dehydration, and if the fever is very high your doctor may suggest an over-the-counter medicine such as acetaminophen or ibuprofen [2]. Adults can also take aspirin, but never give aspirin to a child with fever [2]. Most fevers last 2 to 4 days, and it is common for the temperature not to come all the way down after a fever medicine — that alone does not mean anything more serious [4].

Watch your general condition and your colour, and check for petechiae — small red spots on the skin that do not fade when you press their sides [4].

q: he has an inhaler but I dont know when to use it
text:
A wheeze or asthma flare is usually treated at home with a bronchodilator inhaler like salbutamol, which opens the airways and eases the symptoms, according to the SEUP [4][2]. Give it with a spacer (and a mask for small children), never straight into the mouth — that way more of the medicine reaches the lungs [1][4].

Get help if:
- He is very restless or drowsy, or turns blue or pale [1]
- Breathing gets worse: faster, ribs or chest pulling in, lots of belly movement [1]
- He needs the inhaler every two hours or less [1]
- He can't speak properly or his lips look blue [3]

If there is no clear improvement after using the inhaler, go to a health centre [1]. Bring the spacer with you [1].

q: my 9 month old still has no teeth, is that normal
text:
It is normal for a 9-month-old not to have teeth yet. The first tooth usually shows between 4 and 8 months of age, but this varies, according to MedlinePlus [4].

Until then, wipe your baby's gums with a damp washcloth after each meal [4]. Do not put them to bed with a bottle of milk, juice or sugar water — use only water for bedtime bottles [4]. Once the first tooth appears, switch to a soft toothbrush [4]. Ask your health care provider whether your baby needs oral fluoride [4].

Once teeth come in, brush them at least twice a day, especially before bed, and do the real brushing yourself [1]. Take your child to a dentist every 6 months [1].

q: my child has chickenpox, when can he go back to school
text:
Chickenpox is very contagious, and children usually miss 5 to 6 days of school or childcare because of it, according to the CDC [1]. A person with chickenpox can pass it on until all the spots have crusted over [2].

Keep him home while he still has fluid-filled blisters that have not crusted. The illness usually lasts about 4 to 7 days [1], and he can go back once all the lesions have turned to scabs [2].

For the itch, calamine lotion and oatmeal baths can help, and acetaminophen can help with fever — do not give aspirin, because with chickenpox it can cause Reye's syndrome, according to MedlinePlus [3].

See your doctor if:
- The rash looks infected or very painful [3]
- He has trouble breathing [3]
- He seems very drowsy or confused [3]
- He is not drinking or is getting worse [3]

q: she bumped her forehead on the table and cried right away, do I need to watch her
text:
A bump on the head is usually minor, because the skull is hard and protects the brain, according to MedlinePlus [3]. Most head injuries in children are mild and not dangerous [4].

What to do now: keep her resting, physically and mentally, for 24 to 48 hours depending on how hard the knock was — no sport and no screens during that time [2]. She can sleep, but after a more significant knock it is worth waking her every 4 hours [5]. She can eat and drink as usual, according to her appetite [5]. If she has a headache, paracetamol or ibuprofen can be given in the dose your doctor indicates [5].

Watch her over the first 24 hours [4], and get help if:
- Headache that is intense, getting worse, or not eased by the usual medicine [2]
- Repeated vomiting [2]
- Confusion, or in a very small child, being irritable or hard to wake [2]
- Changes in usual behaviour, trouble speaking or walking [2]
- Blood or clear fluid from the nose or ears [2]

q: I read that vaccines can cause autism, is that actually true
text:
No, that is not true: many scientific studies have looked at this and found no link between vaccines and autism, according to MedlinePlus [1]. Vaccines are safe, and they must go through extensive safety testing and evaluation before they are approved in the United States [1].

If you are wondering when your child should get their vaccines, they are given at well-child visits, following the vaccination schedule [4]. The CDC publishes the schedule for the United States, listing which vaccines are recommended, how many doses are needed and at what age [4]. Following it means your child gets protection against serious diseases at the right time, so their body can build immunity before being exposed [4].

If you have concerns about a specific vaccine or about your child's schedule, talk with your child's doctor.

q: my daughter has a seizure right now, what do I do
banner: 🚨 Call 911 now or go to the emergency department. | Reason: Abnormal movements / seizure
text:
Keep your daughter safe while you wait for help. Lay her on her side in a safe place, away from anything she could hit, and put nothing in her mouth, according to the SEUP [6]. Check the time the seizure starts and ends, and protect her head with your hands or something soft [5].

If the seizure has stopped, put her in the recovery position and make sure nothing in her mouth or throat is blocking her breathing [5]. If she has not had fever medicine in the last 2 hours, you can give paracetamol or ibuprofen [6].

A febrile seizure usually lasts less than 5 minutes, and afterwards a child is often sleepy or confused for a short time [6]. She needs to be checked by a doctor after a first seizure [4][6].

q: my baby is 7 months and has been warm since last night, 101.8 F
text:
A fever is a sign the body is fighting an infection, and most fevers in babies are caused by infections, according to MedlinePlus [1]. Keep offering breast milk or formula often, since fluids help prevent dehydration [1].

For babies, any fever is a reason to see a health professional as soon as possible, according to MedlinePlus [2]. Also get help if your baby:

- is unusually irritable or low on energy [2]
- has fewer wet nappies, or none for 3 hours or more [2][6]
- cries without tears, or has a dry mouth and tongue [6]
- is drowsy, or has sunken eyes [6]
- is breathing fast or has a rapid heartbeat [6]

You can give paracetamol or ibuprofen for a high fever; the dose depends on your baby's weight [1]. Never give aspirin to a child with fever [1].

q: my daughter has diarrhea since yesterday and doesnt want much food
text:
Diarrhea in children is usually caused by a virus and gets better on its own with rest and plenty of fluids, according to MedlinePlus [2][4]. Rotavirus is the most common cause of acute diarrhea in children [4].

Offer fluids and electrolytes often, in small sips, and let her eat what she wants — she may not feel like much food while she is unwell [2]. Probiotics may help shorten a case of diarrhea [2].

Contact a provider right away if she has any of these:
- Change in mental state, such as irritability or lack of energy [3]
- Diarrhea lasting more than a day [3]
- Any fever in an infant, or high fever in an older child [3]
- Frequent loose stools or vomiting often [3]
- Signs of dehydration: thirst, dry mouth, urinating less than usual or no wet diapers for 3 hours or more, no tears when crying [3]

q: is the MMR vaccine safe for my baby I read online it causes autism
text:
No, the MMR vaccine does not cause autism — studies have found no evidence of a link, according to the NHS [1]. The American Academy of Pediatrics, the National Academy of Medicine and the CDC have all concluded that the benefits of vaccines outweigh their risks [3], and many scientific studies have looked at this and found no link between vaccines and autism [5].

MMR protects against measles, mumps and rubella, and most people vaccinated with it are protected for life [6]. Children need 2 doses, usually the first at 12 through 15 months and the second at 4 through 6 years, following the United States national schedule [6]. It can be given at the same time as other vaccines [6].

Serious allergic reactions are rare and usually happen within minutes, when the person who vaccinates your child is trained to treat them straight away [7].

Speak to your doctor if you are worried about your child having a vaccine, or are not sure whether they can have it [7].

q: my baby has yellow skin, is that normal at 3 days old
banner: 🚨 With these symptoms your child should be seen in the emergency department today, without waiting. | Reason: Baby with yellow skin or eyes: urgent appointment today. If under 24 hours old, very sleepy, not feeding, feverish or no wet nappies, go to emergency now
text:
Jaundice at around 3 days old is common in babies, and for most babies the yellow is most noticeable at about this age [1]. It usually clears on its own over about 2 weeks [1].

Because your baby is under 3 months old, they need to be checked by a doctor today. Keep feeding them and keep a note of their wet and dirty nappies [1].

Get help now if your baby:
- is sleepier than normal or hard to wake [1]
- is not feeding [1]
- is floppy or stiff, or has jerking or twitching movements [1]
- has a temperature of 38°C (100.4°F) or more, or 36°C (96.8°F) or less, or feels hot or cold or is shivering [1]
- has no wet nappies, or is breathing with grunting or their stomach sucking in under the ribs [1]

Also tell the doctor if their pee is dark yellow or brown, or their poo is pale and creamy — keep a sample of the poo to show them [1].

text:
If your child is under 3 months old, a fever needs a doctor the same day. For an older child, cold hands and feet with a fever are a sign to take seriously, not something to watch at home — the NHS lists unusually cold hands and feet among the signs that need immediate help [2].

While you get her seen: keep her comfortable, do not undress her or sponge her down to cool her, and do not cover her in too many clothes or bedclothes [2]. Offer fluids often. Do not give aspirin to a child under 16 [2].

Get help now if she also has:
- a stiff neck [2][7]
- a rash that does not fade when pressed [2][7]
- being drowsy and hard to wake, or confused [2][7]
- difficulty breathing [2]
- a fit for the first time [2]

q: my baby is making fewer wet diapers today
banner: 🚨 With these symptoms your child should be seen in the emergency department today, without waiting. | Reason: Signs of dehydration: sunken eyes, little urine, dry mouth, persistent vomiting or heavy diarrhoea >24 h
text:
Fewer wet diapers than usual can be a sign of dehydration, and babies are more at risk of it [4]. In a baby, signs include a sunken soft spot on the head, sunken eyes, few or no tears when crying, fewer wet nappies than usual, and being drowsy or irritable [4].

Keep offering fluids. If your baby is breastfed, keep breastfeeding normally and even more often if they want it [1]. Offer oral rehydration solution in small amounts, and keep feeding a nearly normal diet in smaller, more frequent amounts [1][7]. Avoid sports drinks, sweets and juices [1].

Get help today if your baby has a dry mouth and tongue, cries without tears, has had no wet diaper for 3 hours or more, is unusually sleepy or irritable, or has sunken eyes [6]. Also get help if they refuse to eat or drink, or are very irritable or hard to wake [7].

q: she feels hot but the thermometer says 98.6
text:
A temperature of 98.6°F is normal, not a fever — a normal temperature is generally around 98.6°F or 37°C (98.6 °F), according to MedlinePlus [5]. A fever is a body temperature higher than normal, and it is usually a sign the body is fighting an infection [5]. If she feels hot to touch but the thermometer reads normal, she may just feel warm; a high temperature is 38°C (100.4 °F) or more [1].

What you can do: make sure she is drinking plenty of fluids to stay hydrated, keep her in a room that is a neutral, ventilated temperature, and avoid wrapping her in too many clothes or blankets so she can lose heat [3]. It is normal for her to have less appetite — do not force her to eat [3]. If she is uncomfortable, paracetamol or ibuprofen can be given at the dose your doctor recommends, every 6 to 8 hours [3]. Do not give aspirin to a child under 16 [7].

Watch for: a rash that does not fade when you press a glass against it [7]; a stiff neck, being bothered by light, or a first seizure [7]; drowsiness that is hard to wake, confusion, or unusual cold hands and feet [7]; difficulty breathing [7]; a fever lasting 5 days or more [7].

text:
A swallowed magnet needs medical assessment, and more than one magnet is a particular concern: swallowing several magnetic pieces can cause twisting of the bowel, according to Ecimed [6]. A single magnet usually causes no problem [6].

While you get help, do not try to make your child vomit, and do not give water, milk, oil or any food, according to the SEUP [3]. If you can see a solid object in the mouth and can reach it, take it out — never blindly, as that could make things worse [3]. Try to work out how much was swallowed [3].

The SEUP advises going to the emergency department after swallowing an object, especially batteries or magnets [5]. If your child does not respond normally, is not breathing well or has a bad colour, call your local emergency number [3].

q: my child has a rash after having a fever, could it be from the fever
text:
If your child is under 3 months old, a fever needs a doctor the same day.

A rash that appears just as the fever drops is typical of roseola, a common viral illness in babies and toddlers. According to the SEUP, the usual pattern is high fever for 3 to 4 days with no other symptoms, then the fever falls and a faint, flat, widespread rash appears that is not itchy and lasts about 48 hours [2]. It is diagnosed by this sequence of events, and there is no vaccine to prevent it [2].

There is no specific treatment for the rash itself. If the fever is making your child uncomfortable, paracetamol is the first choice and ibuprofen is an option; the dose depends on your child's age and weight, so use the dose your doctor or the leaflet gives [5].

Get help if:
- Your child is floppy, barely responsive or very irritable [1]
- Breathing is difficult [1]
- Spots do not fade when you press them [1]
- Your child cannot keep down solids or fluids [1]
- Fever lasts more than 5 days [6]

q: what are the side effects of chickenpox shot
text:
Most side effects of the chickenpox vaccine are mild and do not last long, according to the CDC. They can include pain or swelling where the shot was given, a mild fever, and a rash at the injection site or, less often, elsewhere on the body — usually within a month of vaccination [1]. Serious reactions, such as a severe allergic reaction, are very rare, and the person who gives the vaccine is trained to treat them right away [1].

The chickenpox vaccine is given on the United States schedule, so ask your doctor which doses your child needs and when [1].

Get medical help if:
- A severe allergic reaction (trouble breathing, swelling of the face or throat, widespread hives) [1]
- A rash that spreads or does not go away [1]
- Your child seems very unwell after the shot [1]

q: my baby has a cough and sounds very congested when sleeping
text:
For a baby with a cough and a blocked, congested nose at night, the usual cause is a common cold, and it is not a sign of anything serious [7]. Keep your baby sleeping on their back on a firm, flat mattress, with pillows, sheets and blankets kept away from them [1]. The safest place for them to sleep is a separate cot or Moses basket free from toys, blankets and pillows [3]. If you share a bed, do not swaddle them, and keep other children and pets out of the bed [1].

Get urgent help if:
- your baby is struggling for breath [7]
- your baby stops breathing or will not wake up [7]
- your baby's lips, tongue, face or skin turn pale, blue or grey [7]
- your baby is limp, floppy or not responding as usual [7]
- you are worried about your baby or think they might be ill [7]

q: my 10 month old is pulling his ear and crying a lot
text:
Ear infections are a common cause of ear pulling and crying in babies, and most clear up on their own within about 3 days, according to the NHS [3]. Other signs to look for are fluid draining from the ear, trouble sleeping, and being irritable or restless [3][4].

For the pain, you can give paracetamol or ibuprofen; the right dose depends on your child's weight, and PediBot's dose calculator can work it out for you [6]. Do not put anything inside the ear to ease the pain, and keep the ear dry, especially if it has been discharging [6]. If your baby is still feeding, frequent saline nose drops can help [6].

See your doctor if:
- The pain or crying is getting worse, or lasts more than a few days [3]
- There is discharge, pus or fluid coming from the ear [3][4]
- Your baby has a high temperature or seems very unwell [3]
- Your baby is not feeding or is hard to wake [3]

q: my 3 year old keeps vomiting every time he drinks water
text:
Vomiting that happens every time he drinks is a sign he is not keeping fluids down, and the SEUP lists vomiting a lot, or not tolerating liquids, as a reason to be seen in an emergency department [2].

While you get help, offer small sips of water rather than a full glass, or ice chips to suck, which is what MedlinePlus suggests when liquids will not stay down [1]. The NHS also advises small sips of rehydration solution to replace lost fluids, and says not to give young children fruit juice or fizzy drinks, as these can make vomiting worse [3].

Get help now if:
- He vomits even when he takes nothing [2]
- Vomit is green, bloody, or looks like coffee grounds [2]
- He is drowsy, limp, very thirsty, has sunken eyes, cries without tears, or passes little urine [2]
- Severe tummy pain or headache [2]
